newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks surge as Chidambaram spreads cheer.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks surge as Chidambaram spreads cheer.

text.p: Indian stocks surged two percent on Wednesday as former finance minister P. Chidambaram's return to the government spread cheer across markets, traders said.

"It's a good move and should boost investor confidence," said Aditya Rattan, chief representative at Daiwa Securities, referring to the Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) party's decision to rejoin the government.

Chidambaram -- a member of the regional party which opted to stay out of the new government earlier this month after TMC leader G.K. Moopanar was passed over in the choice for Prime Minister -- is due to be sworn in as finance minister.
Bombay's benchmark stocks index jumped 70.56 points, or 1.85 percent, to 3879.21 minutes after a delayed opening as investors and speculators bid furiously on the news.
But early gains were capped as speculators booked profits and the index fell back slightly to 3858.33.
The widely-tracked index has been rangebound during the last seven trading sessions as most investors crossed their fingers and opted to sit on the sidelines until Chidambaram returned.
"Investors like his aggression, his ability to take hard decisions," said a local fund manager, citing Chidambaram's path-breaking federal budget, announced on February 28.

Parliament on Wednesday opened a two-and-a-half week session to debate the 1997/98 (April-March) budget which slashed taxes, upped foreign portfolio limits in stocks of Indian companies and proposed allowing firms to buyback their shares.
"With the comeback of Chidambaram as finance minister, the financial budget would be passed without any major amendments," said Manoj Choraria of brokers Choraria Investments in Delhi.
In its cover story "The Importance of Being Chidambaram," news magazine Outlook asked leading industrialists why so many people believed the former finance minister was indispensible to the economy.
"Chidambaram is a gentleman, he is easy to deal with, he is straightforward and progressive," responded top industrialist Ratan Tata, who heads the Tata group.

Delhi's index jumped 16.78 points, or 2.1 percent, to 815.40 in early trade as investors bought on hopes that Chidambaram would pilot the budget through parliament, despite opposition from Left parties and rightwing opposition Bharatiya Janata Party. Both groups have said they plan to oppose various budget proposals.
On the National Stock Exchange (NSE), the index traded 23.30 points, or 2.2 percent, higher at 1080.75 -- off its early high of 1088.15.
Analysts said fundamental factors like falling interest rates -- triggered by an easier central bank monetary policy announced earlier this month -- would also drive stocks higher.
"We expect interest rates to decline, especially at the long end, triggering a rally in stocks," Morgan Stanley analyst Pravin Shah said in a country report.
Most banks have cut their prime lending rates to 14.0-16 percent from 14.5-17.5 percent.

Prateek Agarwal, deputy manager research at SBI Capital Markets, forecast Bombay's index would rise to 4500 points in the next three months as investors discounted poor company results for 1996/97 and looked ahead.
"There will be some sluggishness due to the results but then people will start looking at 1997/98 numbers and focus on interest rates which are close to all-time lows."
